aiPrompt.systemPrompt: You are a master middle school math teacher.
aiPrompt.mainPrompt: Below is a student's mathematics document, as a text summary, a picture, or both. Either may be absent. Evaluate and categorize it.
aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the document based on its content and the general proportional reasoning curriculum found in middle grades mathematics.
aiPrompt.keyIndicatorsPrompt: Return exactly one item: a single sentence of at most 30 words, written to the student as "you", saying why this category fits by naming one specific thing in their document - a number, ratio, label, table column, or phrase they actually wrote. Do not restate the problem, summarize the document as a whole, or explain the mathematics in general.

CQ Problem 4.4 Making Sense of Percent Situations
CQ Comparing Quantities ACE Question Banks

aiUnitSummary.overview: Comparing Quantities is the grade 6 unit where ratio reasoning begins, built around a school fundraiser. Investigation 1 separates additive from multiplicative comparison — "$150 more than" against "for every $60, $90" — names the second a ratio, and distinguishes part-to-part from part-to-whole and equivalent ratios from merely different-looking ones. Investigation 2 uses ratios to answer questions, moving from scaling by a common factor to ratio tables, then to an equation and graph of the same relationship, with tape diagrams introduced through sharing a segmented smoothie bar. Investigation 3 isolates the unit rate, shows that every ratio has two of them, and applies rate tables and unit rates to popcorn, slime recipes and backward walking speeds. Investigation 4 introduces percent as a part-to-whole ratio scaled to a whole of 100, with 100-grids, tape diagrams and the 1% mark as the tools. Throughout, students judge written claims about the same data and decide which are ratios and which are true.

entries.priorKnowledge: From grade 5 and the Number Connections unit: multiplication and division of whole numbers and simple fractions; factors and multiples; equivalent fractions; reading a simple table. Ratio language is not assumed — this problem is explicitly a pre-assessment of how students already compare quantities.
entries.problemDigest: Opens the unit with eight written claims comparing three schools' fundraising goals, and asks students to decide whether each is true and which ones actually compare two quantities. The claims are deliberately mixed: some additive ("$150 more than"), some multiplicative ("for every $60, $90"), some fractional, some percent, one with the two quantities named in the wrong order, and one — "Central will raise the most" — that is true but compares nothing. The What If section has students try to rewrite each claim as a "for every" statement and find that absolute statements cannot be, ask whether a subtraction statement is still a comparison, and decide whether a true statement is necessarily a comparison. The problem is a pre-assessment: the vocabulary comes later.
entries.approachGuidance: This is a pre-assessment and students' comparison language is expected to be informal and varied. Draw out their own way of comparing rather than introducing ratio vocabulary.

entries.priorKnowledge: That a comparison can be additive or multiplicative, and that some true statements compare nothing at all; the fundraising context; from Number Connections, factors, multiples and the multiplicative structure of number; equivalent fractions.
entries.problemDigest: Defines a ratio as a comparison of two quantities by multiplicative thinking, contrasted directly with additive comparison — the change from 2 to 10 as multiplying by 5 rather than adding 8. Students then sort eight claims about pizza preference, deciding for each whether it is a ratio and which two quantities it compares: "for every 10 who prefer cheese, 5 prefer pepperoni" is one, while "2/3 of the students prefer cheese" is a fraction of a whole rather than a comparison of two quantities, though it can be rewritten as one. The What If section works on whether claims that look different are equivalent, scaling 2-to-1 up to 10-to-5, and on a pair that express the same relationship with the quantities named in the opposite order.
entries.approachGuidance: Students are expected to rely on "for every" language rather than a formal definition, and more than one wording is correct. Do not push toward a single preferred form.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio as a multiplicative comparison of two quantities; equivalent ratios found by scaling both quantities by the same factor; that the order of a ratio matters only if the quantities are labelled correctly; additive comparisons and why they differ.
entries.problemDigest: Separates part-to-part from part-to-whole ratios using boxes of green and white cupcakes — a large box of 8 green and 10 white, a small box of 4 green and 8 white. Students write as many ratio statements as they can about and between the boxes, then compare with classmates and decide which are equivalent, which surfaces how many different true statements one situation supports. The What If section gives six claims about a box and asks students to agree or disagree, say which are ratios, and write an equivalent for one: among them a correct part-to-whole, one with the quantities switched, one stating a difference rather than a ratio, and one confusing a part-to-part ratio with a fraction of the whole.
entries.approachGuidance: The challenge asks for as many ratio statements as students can write, and comparing the variety is the point. Accept any correctly labelled statement rather than a canonical one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratios as multiplicative comparisons; part-to-part and part-to-whole forms; equivalent ratios and scaling both quantities by a common factor; the several notations for a ratio, including "for every", "to", "per" and the colon form; that additive adjustment changes a ratio.
entries.problemDigest: Turns ratio from a way of describing to a way of solving. The students have 40 white cupcakes and must work out how many green cupcakes and how many boxes are needed, for both the large box (8 green to 10 white) and the small (4 green to 8 white), and then say which operations they used. The What If section compares three students' strategies, including one that is wrong in an instructive way: Zane multiplies both quantities by 4; Yvonne adds 30 to each, reasoning additively, and so gets 38 green to 40 white — a mixture with far more green than the original. Working out why Yvonne's answer is wrong is where the multiplicative nature of a ratio becomes concrete.
entries.approachGuidance: Several correct scaling strategies are compared alongside an incorrect additive one. Help students see why a strategy works rather than supplying the arithmetic.

entries.priorKnowledge: Using equivalent ratios to solve problems; scaling both quantities by a common factor, up or down; that additive adjustment does not preserve a ratio; reading and extending a simple table; plotting points on a coordinate grid.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces the ratio table as an organised record of equivalent ratios, then connects it to an equation and a graph. Students use a partly filled table of boxes sold against money collected to find the cost of 20, 60, 12 and 1 box, which raises why dividing is legitimate in a multiplicative situation — dividing by 2 and multiplying by one half being the same move — and why knowing the cost of one box is especially useful. The What If section follows Hazel, who writes A = 12N from the table and sketches its graph, and asks what 240 = 12N is asking for, what shape the graph takes and why, and what each of the three representations is good and bad at.
entries.approachGuidance: Table, equation and graph are compared for their advantages, with no single best one. Move between representations rather than settling on one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Equivalent ratios, ratio tables and scaling; the connection between a ratio table, an equation of the form y = ax and its graph; partitioning a whole into equal parts; simple fractions of a quantity.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces the tape diagram through sharing a segmented smoothie bar in the ratio of two people's ages. Sofia, 12, and Dembe, 6, share a bar of 9 segments, and students decide how to partition it — the ratio 12 to 6 reduces to 2 to 1, so the bar splits 6 and 3. The harder case follows: the same ratio applied to a 4-segment bar, which forces each segment to be subdivided into thirds, making the point that the size of a piece does not matter as long as the multiplicative relationship holds. The What If section asks how many segments a bar must have for a 10-year-old and a 15-year-old to share without new cuts, leading to multiples of 5, and asks for three equivalent ratios describing the split.
entries.approachGuidance: Partitioning can be done in several valid ways and students are asked to show their thinking. Support the partition a student devised rather than a tidier one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Equivalent ratios, scaling, ratio tables, tape diagrams, and the equation and graph of a ratio relationship; that one quantity in a ratio can be scaled to a convenient value; multiplying and dividing to find equivalent ratios.
entries.problemDigest: Defines the unit rate — a ratio in which one quantity is 1 — and uses it to solve. Six boxes of smoothie bars sell for $48, and students find the cost per box, the number of boxes sold for $104, and the money from 20 boxes, explaining their reasoning each time. The What If section sets three strategies side by side: Brandon builds a rate table down to the unit rate and scales from there, Sofia steps through multiples of the original ratio, and Kaedon writes C = 8N. All three work, but the discussion draws out that Sofia's multiples skip past both $104 and 20 boxes, so she would need to scale down to smaller values — an argument for the unit rate rather than a rule.
entries.approachGuidance: Three valid strategies are compared, and the limits of one are the lesson. Help students weigh when a strategy is convenient rather than ranking them.

entries.priorKnowledge: Unit rate as a ratio with one quantity equal to 1, and its use in rate tables and equations; equivalent ratios and scaling; that a rate compares quantities measured in different units; simple fractions as multipliers.
entries.problemDigest: Extends unit rates to rates proper, where the two quantities carry different units — miles per hour, cups per ounce. One ounce of kernels makes 4 cups of popcorn, and students use a rate table to find the cups from 12 and 30 ounces and the ounces needed for 40 and 100 cups, extending and scaling the table where the value is not already in it. The What If section examines Zena's use of unit rates in both directions, and then Will's claim that 1 cup per quarter-ounce is also a unit rate — establishing that every ratio has two unit rates and that which one is convenient depends on the question being asked. Students build a rate table from Will's version.
entries.approachGuidance: Both unit rates are valid and the useful one depends on the question. Help students choose between them rather than fixing on one orientation.

entries.priorKnowledge: Unit rates in both directions and rate tables; scaling ratios up and down, including by fractions; that dividing by a number and multiplying by its reciprocal are the same; measuring quantities in a recipe.
entries.problemDigest: Applies ratio reasoning to a recipe that has gone wrong. A slime recipe pairs 2 bottles of glue with 1 teaspoon of baking soda; Zack has already put in 3 bottles and 1 teaspoon, and students work out what to add — the ratio needs 1.5 teaspoons, so half a teaspoon more. The What If section scales the whole recipe down by a half, which requires halving quantities given in fractions, and then scales a different ratio up: 2 containers of slime for every 3 children, applied to 30 children. The problem is short and is mainly practice at choosing among the strategies built in the previous two problems.
entries.approachGuidance: Students pick their own route through each adjustment, and several are listed as expected. Support the strategy chosen rather than naming a preferred one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Unit rates in both directions, rate tables and scaling, including with fractional quantities; rates with different units; writing equivalent ratios; that comparing rates may require scaling one quantity to a common value.
entries.problemDigest: Compares rates that are not obviously comparable. Wilson walks backward a quarter-mile in 5 minutes and Sam a fifth of a mile in 4 minutes, and students decide who is faster — the answer being neither, since both reduce to a twentieth of a mile per minute, reachable by scaling either the distance to 1 mile or the time to 1 minute. The What If section takes the average rate of a quarter-mile in 6 minutes and asks for the distance covered in a 30-minute race, the time for a full mile, the rate in feet per minute, the distance at 3 mph, and the race winner's rate in miles per hour — a sequence that requires converting units as well as scaling.
entries.approachGuidance: The two walkers turn out to be equally fast, and students may reach that by scaling either quantity. Follow the comparison a student set up rather than redirecting it.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratios, equivalent ratios and scaling; part-to-whole comparison; unit rates and rate tables; that scaling one quantity of a ratio to a convenient value makes two ratios comparable; reading a 10-by-10 grid.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces percent as a part-to-whole ratio whose whole has been scaled to 100. Seventy-eight of 100 sixth graders liked the fundraiser, which students represent by shading a 100-grid and a bar. The instructive case follows: 38 of 50 seventh graders, which is shaded as two groups of 38 out of 50 to reach 76 out of 100 — and the text flags that this is not adding fractions but scaling both quantities of a ratio. Students then compare the two groups, which is the point of a common whole. The What If section reads four percent diagrams with different numbers of divisions, including one of 25 boxes where each box is 4%, and asks for a ratio statement and a problem for each.
entries.approachGuidance: Diagrams can be read in several ways and students invent problems of their own. Support the reading a student offers rather than converting straight to a calculation.

entries.priorKnowledge: Percent as a part-to-whole ratio with a whole of 100; representing percents on 100-grids and bars; equivalent ratios, scaling and unit rates; the tape-diagram idea from sharing smoothie bars.
entries.problemDigest: Builds strategies for finding a percent when the whole is not 100. Survey data from a class is analysed, with the worked case being 136 out of 400 students preferring tacos. The What If section compares four students' methods and asks how they are alike: Suri and Zane both use tape diagrams, Zane and Julia both work out what 1% represents, and Kelly scales the ratio directly to a whole of 100. A second survey — 117 of 180 saying yes — is then worked two ways, including by bracketing between 50%, 60% and 70% of 180 before refining with the 1% value. Finding 1% first emerges here as the general-purpose move.
entries.approachGuidance: Four strategies are compared and students relate them to their own, with efficiency rather than correctness the distinction. Avoid prescribing one method.

entries.priorKnowledge: Percent as a part-to-whole ratio scaled to 100; tape diagrams, 100-grids and double number lines; finding what 1% represents and scaling from it; equivalent ratios and unit rates.
entries.problemDigest: Applies percent to genetic traits — attached earlobes, tongue curling and others — using data from one classroom. Students find what percent of the class has each trait, then use those percents to predict how many of the school's 250 students would, which is scaling a sample proportion up to a population. The What If section works through Marjorie's tape diagram in the reverse direction: given marks for 1% and 10%, students work out the school's size, how she found the 10% mark, how many students cannot curl their tongue, and what percent that is. The closing discussion draws the explicit parallel between the 1% mark and a unit rate.
entries.approachGuidance: The diagram can be entered at several points and students are asked for other ways to find the percent. Follow the route a student takes through it.

entries.priorKnowledge: Percent as a part-to-whole ratio with a whole of 100; finding a percent when the whole is not 100, including by way of the 1% value; tape diagrams and 100-grids; unit rates and rate tables; comparing ratios by scaling to a common whole.
entries.problemDigest: Applies percent across several everyday situations and confronts a common misreading. Baruti got exactly one question wrong on every assignment, and students find the ratio of correct to total points and the percent for each — which exposes that one wrong out of 2 and one wrong out of 25 are very different despite the identical difference, since a percent compares the quantities multiplicatively. The problem then moves through further contexts in which percent is used day to day. It closes Investigation 4 by consolidating the distinction the unit opened with, now in percent form: a constant difference does not mean a constant comparison.
entries.approachGuidance: The point is why equal differences give unequal percents. Support reasoning about the comparison rather than confirming the arithmetic.

entries.priorKnowledge: The whole unit: additive against multiplicative comparison; ratio, equivalent ratios, part-to-part and part-to-whole; scaling, ratio tables, tape diagrams, equations and graphs; unit rates in both directions and rate tables; percent as a part-to-whole ratio with a whole of 100, and finding a percent through the 1% value.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's four Mathematical Reflections, one per investigation, each asking what students understand about ratios and reasoning with ratios. The expected ground accumulates across them: that comparisons may be additive or multiplicative and serve different purposes; that a ratio expresses the multiplicative relationship and may be written with raw or scaled values, part-to-part or part-to-whole; that equivalent ratios share a common multiplicative factor and that ratio tables organise them; that every ratio has two unit rates and that these connect to expressions, equations and graphs; and that percents are part-to-whole ratios with a whole of 100, which is what makes two ratios with different wholes comparable.

entries.priorKnowledge: Whatever has been covered when the exercises are assigned; the banks are organised by investigation and are normally used alongside the corresponding problems rather than after the whole unit.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's ACE question banks — Applications, Connections and Extensions — gathered as one item and grouped by investigation rather than taught as a problem. Investigation 1's bank asks students to write their own comparison statements about fundraising goals, both additive and multiplicative, and to judge whether a given "for every" statement describes a stated count of pens and pencils. Investigation 2's bank covers scaling ratios in context: carnations to roses in a bouquet, defective light bulbs at 2 per 1,000 scaled to a billion, and walking distances at a steady pace. Investigation 3's bank works on unit rates in both directions and on completing ratio comparison statements from tabulated survey data. Later banks cover percent.
